lesson.title: Climbing Uphill: Endothermic Energy Diagrams
lesson.summary: In an endothermic reaction, the products end up at higher potential energy than the reactants, so the reaction coordinate diagram finishes above where it started, showing energy absorbed from the surroundings.
lesson.body:
An endothermic diagram is the mirror image of an exothermic one. The reactants are drawn at a starting height, the curve climbs to a peak, the transition state, and Ea forward is measured from the reactants up to that peak, exactly as before. What differs is what happens after the peak: instead of dropping below the starting height, the curve only comes partway down, ending at a products level that sits above the reactants. That upward shift from reactants to products is delta H, and for an endothermic reaction delta H is positive, because the system absorbed energy from its surroundings rather than releasing it. A second consequence follows directly from the geometry: since the products are now closer to the peak than the reactants are, Ea for the reverse reaction is smaller than Ea for the forward reaction, the opposite pattern from the exothermic case.

A clean real example is the thermal decomposition of limestone in a lime kiln, calcium carbonate breaking down into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide gas, CaCO3 solid forming CaO solid plus CO2 gas, with delta H around positive 178 kJ per mole. On the diagram, solid CaCO3 starts low, the curve climbs to a peak, Ea, and then settles at a products level, CaO plus CO2, that sits noticeably higher than the starting reactant. In practice this means the kiln must keep supplying heat continuously. If the heat source is removed, the reaction simply stops, because the products are higher in energy than the reactants and the system has no built in energy source of its own to keep climbing.

This ties back to what endothermic reactions mean at the level of bonds: breaking the bonds in the reactants costs more energy than is recovered when the new bonds in the products form, so the reaction needs a net energy input from outside to proceed. That energy has to come from somewhere, a flame under a kiln, heat from a water bath, or in a very different setting, sunlight.

It helps to clear up a common misconception here: an uphill diagram does not mean a reaction cannot happen, only that it will not happen on its own without an energy source, and that once it does happen it draws energy in rather than giving it off. Photosynthesis is a good large-scale illustration. Plants convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen, 6CO2 plus 6H2O forming C6H12O6 plus 6O2, and because this is the reverse of glucose combustion, whose delta H is about negative 2803 kJ per mole, photosynthesis itself is endothermic by about positive 2803 kJ per mole of glucose formed. The energy that gets absorbed is light energy from the sun, captured by chlorophyll and stored in the chemical bonds of glucose, which is precisely what the upward path on an endothermic diagram represents: energy taken in from the surroundings and locked into the products.
